abstract: This conceptual review examines how political science and communication scholars use the label 'non-political' and how they draw boundaries between the political and the nonpolitical. Drawing on a relational (rather than substantialist) understanding of politics, the authors conduct a boundary analysis of 140 empirical studies, identifying two dominant conceptual 'treatments' of the nonpolitical — categorical and contextual — along with the relational modes that link political and nonpolitical domains. They argue that attending to the nonpolitical and to (de)politicization offers a heuristic, indirect route to reflecting on the nature of politics itself, and call for a more active reconciliation of the two treatments.
key_claims: The traditional presupposition of politics as a self-contained, bounded sphere is being disrupted, yet growing scholarly interest in the nonpolitical lacks conceptual clarity and consistent theoretical justification.

A relational ontology — in which the political is constituted through its differentiating relations with nonpolitical domains rather than through intrinsic features — is essential and preferable to a substantialist view for analyzing the nonpolitical.

Scholarly uses of the 'non-political' label fall into two broad treatments: a categorical one (an inherent, stable, exclusive feature) and a contextual one (a temporary, transformative, context-dependent state).

The way scholars construct the political/nonpolitical boundary is shaped by intellectual traditions, theoretical orientations, methodological standards, and rhetorical norms of academic knowledge production, not purely by empirical necessity.

(De)politicization should be recognized as a meaningful relational and meta-theoretical analytical lens, and boundary-drawing between political and nonpolitical should be understood as a power-laden, inherently political act.
The nonpolitical is unlikely to become a standalone empirical subfield, but studying it yields epistemological reflection on the nature of politics — 'the politics of the non-political.'
methods: A genealogical review of the nature of politics in political theory (Plato, Aristotle, Augustine, Hegel, liberalism/Ryan, Schmitt, Wolin, feminist theory, new social movements, Foucault, relational theorists such as Emirbayer and Selg & Ventsel).
Boundary analysis grounded in a relational ontology, treating 'non-political' as a boundary object (Star) rather than a mature analytical concept.
A systematic literature search in Web of Science using three keyword sets: non-political/nonpolitical, apolitical, and non-news (where news is treated as politics).

Scope limited to English-language SSCI articles in political science and communication, 2004–2024, yielding 448 articles; screening for empirical evidence, exclusion of purely journalism 'non-news' work, and retention of journals with more than five sample articles produced a final sample of 140 articles.

Inductive coding to characterize how scholars delineate the boundary and nature of the nonpolitical, recurring relational mechanisms linking nonpolitical and political, and stated motivations, problematizations, and implications.
findings: Roughly two-thirds of the articles adopt a categorical treatment, operationalizing the nonpolitical as a binary, either-or category — sometimes residually (what remains after accounting for political elements) and sometimes substantively (the private, mundane/entertainment, politically neutral, or nonpartisan).

Categorical work is associated with relational modes of spillover/invasion (including a 'backward spillover' from nonpolitical to political) and comparison (treating political and nonpolitical as stable, internally coherent domains placed side by side).

The contextual treatment views the nonpolitical as a temporary, hybrid, transformative state, associated with the relational modes of (de)politicization (processual transformation driven by media, elites/institutions, and grassroots actors) and embeddedness (political meanings embedded within ostensibly nonpolitical settings, e.g., 'third spaces' and intertextuality).

Categorical distinctions are more common in quantitative/post-positivist work, while contextual fluidity is emphasized in interpretive and critical work; some studies pragmatically reconcile them via hedging language ('ostensibly,' 'seemingly') and spectrum/gradational measures of 'politicalness.'
Political Behavior (15 articles) and Political Communication (11 articles) published the most studies in the sample.

Boundaries exist because they serve theoretical coherence, methodological classification needs ('all models are wrong but some are useful'), and rhetorical functions of signaling novelty — but these can essentialize the nonpolitical and conceal embedded political meaning or power relations.
contributions: Identifies and organizes a fragmented literature by distinguishing two conceptual treatments (categorical and contextual) and four relational modes (spillover/invasion, comparison, (de)politicization, embeddedness) through which the political and nonpolitical are linked.

Provides a relational, boundary-analysis framework for understanding how and why scholars demarcate the nonpolitical, offering new directions for extending political communication research into nonpolitical domains.

Offers practical operational guidance: using 'non-political' labels more thoughtfully, clarifying criteria and level of analysis, and moving from binary toward continuous/gradational measures of political relevance, especially in computational research.

Reclaims (de)politicization as a meta-theoretical, power-sensitive relational lens, calling for processual explanations of how and for whom political meanings emerge rather than treating politicization only as an outcome.
Advances epistemological reflection on the nature of politics by 'decentering the political' and theorizing 'the politics of the non-political.'
framing: The paper positions itself within political communication and political theory debates over 'what the political is' (Delli Carpini; Lane & Coles), explicitly adopting a relational ontology of politics (Emirbayer; Selg & Ventsel; Esposito) against substantialist, institution-centered conceptions. It draws on boundary-work and boundary-object scholarship (Abbott; Star) and theories of symbolic power (Bourdieu; Coles et al.) to treat the political/nonpolitical boundary as a relationally produced, contested site of knowledge production.
